tur33-1: Poor posture, muscle spasm due to pain or a difference in leg length can also make the spine look tilted to one side. In these functional curves there is no rotation of the vertebrae, and the curve corrects when the cause is removed, for example when standing up straight, sitting or lying down. In true (structural) scoliosis, by contrast, a hump appears on one side of the back when bending forward. According to the SRS, a leg length difference does not cause scoliosis; however, a large difference can make a curve look more pronounced.
tur33-2: Forward bend testIf one side of the back rises when bending forward, there may be rotation of the trunk; the diagnosis is made with an X-ray. A scoliometer measures this difference in degrees.

tur33-5: In 966 students aged 10–16 in Portugal, bag weight and postural habits were not linked to scoliosis; poor sitting and standing habits, however, were linked to low back pain. This is a cross-sectional study; it does not show cause and effect, and scoliosis was assessed only with a scoliometer, not confirmed by X-ray.
tur33-6: In one study, generalised joint hypermobility (excessive joint mobility due to connective tissue laxity) was present in 51.4% of 70 children with idiopathic scoliosis and in 19% of their healthy peers; joint hypermobility was not related to the size of the curve. This is a case-control study; it does not show that joint hypermobility causes scoliosis. The authors recommend assessing these children for joint hypermobility and taking it into account when planning physiotherapy.
tur33-7: In young people going through a growth spurt, one-sided habits such as always sitting at the desk leaning to the same side or against a wall, always putting the weight on the same buttock, or always carrying a bag on the same shoulder or a heavy item or musical instrument on the same side can make postural asymmetry more noticeable. When connective tissue flexibility is also present, as in benign joint hypermobility syndrome (now called hypermobility spectrum disorder), we see that these asymmetries and back pain can be more marked. This does not mean that one-sided habits cause structural scoliosis; but it is a good reason to share the load between both sides during the growth years.
tur33-8: In BrAIST, the curve did not reach 50 degrees in 72% of those wearing a brace and 48% of those observed (75% versus 42% in the randomised group alone). The brace was prescribed for at least 18 hours a day; in those who actually wore it for an average of 13 hours or more a day, success was 90–93%.
tur33-9: These exercises are based on three main principles: correcting the trunk yourself in three dimensions, holding the corrected posture, and carrying this posture into daily life (sitting, carrying a bag, studying). Patient education goes alongside them. There are seven well-known schools worldwide: Lyon (France), Schroth (Germany), SEAS (Italy), Barcelona (BSPTS, Spain), Dobomed and FITS (Poland) and Side Shift (UK). In the Schroth method, breathing directed according to the direction of rotation is also part of the programme.

tur33-11: The exercises below, on the other hand, are general exercises that work both sides of the body equally. As long as they do not cause pain, you can usually do them safely; they strengthen the trunk muscles and support posture, but they do not correct the curve on their own and do not replace scoliosis-specific exercises. If you have had spinal surgery or have pain spreading to the leg, talk to your doctor before starting. If pain increases, or if numbness and tingling occur in the arms or legs, stop the exercise and talk to your doctor.
tur33-12: Two types are most common in adults: idiopathic scoliosis that starts in adolescence and progresses slowly, and degenerative scoliosis that develops later in life due to wear of the discs and small joints. According to the SRS, the risk of low back pain with curves under 30 degrees is similar to that of people without scoliosis; with untreated curves over 50–60 degrees, low back pain is more likely.
